clue.text: Set off for assignation outside college

indicators.note: outside tells us the date wraps around the college, the school's letters sitting within it

parts.note: an assignation is a romantic meeting, a date
Eton is the famous English public school, officially Eton College

explanation.surface: Someone heads off for a romantic meeting somewhere beyond the college grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' reads as departing, but it is the definition in its explosive sense. ETON is the English school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off a bomb is to explode it, which is the same as making it blow up.

clue.text: Physician — one for each man of the cloth

parts.note: DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor, a physician
one is a, as in a single item
per means for each, as in 'ten pounds per head'

explanation.surface: A doctor is assigned to every clergyman, one apiece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man of the cloth' normally means a clergyman; here it is a dealer in cloth, a British term for a fabric seller.
explanation.definitionFit: A draper sells textiles, so he is literally a man whose trade is fabric.

clue.text: Attempt to retain the wood? It's worthless

indicators.note: to retain means to keep hold of, so the attempt holds the wood within it

parts.note: an attempt is a try
ash is a tree and its timber, so a wood

explanation.surface: Someone tries to keep some timber, only to be told it's rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Something trashy is cheap and of poor quality, of no value.

clue.text: She's turned brown? Not true!

indicators.note: turned signals that the colour word is read backwards

parts.note: tan is a shade of brown
something not true is a lie, a falsehood

explanation.surface: Someone claims a woman has gone brown, and the reply is a flat denial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses TAN to NAT; 'Not true!' is A LIE, the exclamation one uses to call a statement false.
explanation.definitionFit: Natalie is a woman's first name, so it can stand for 'she'.

clue.text: Only a minor branch, you understand?

definitions.meaning: a small slender shoot of a tree
an informal British verb meaning to grasp or catch on

explanation.surface: A tiny offshoot, and a question checking whether the listener has grasped it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small shoot on a tree is a twig, and in British slang to twig something is to grasp it suddenly.

clue.text: After false move do retreat: support called for

parts.note: a trip is a stumble or slip, a false move

indicators.note: retreat means go back, so the little word do is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: After a stumble, someone is told to back off, and a prop is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreat' sends the little word backwards; 'called for' is padding that leads to the definition, which is a three-legged stand.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-legged stand holds up a camera or telescope, so it is a support.

clue.text: Grub taking end of plant — part vital to growth

parts.note: to rootle is to grub about, digging as a pig does with its snout

indicators.note: end of picks out only the closing letter of the word plant

explanation.surface: A larva eats the tip of a plant, damaging an organ essential to growth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' looks like a noun, a larva, but it is the verb: to dig about.
explanation.definitionFit: A small offshoot of a root draws water and nutrients for the plant, so it is essential to the plant growing.

clue.text: Endless suffering after being incarcerated by military leadership

indicators.note: after puts the shortened suffering behind the imprisoned piece

parts.note: pent, as in pent up, means shut in or confined

indicators.note: endless means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: agony is great suffering

explanation.surface: A prisoner's ceaseless torment at the hands of army chiefs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' cuts AGONY to AGON. The Pentagon is the headquarters of the US Department of Defense, so it stands for the American military command.
explanation.definitionFit: The US defence headquarters building gives its name to the top brass who work there.

clue.text: Language from place down under prince used in broadcast

parts.note: Dis is the classical underworld, a place below ground
Erse is the Gaelic language of Scotland or Ireland

explanation.surface: A tongue from Australia, used by a prince on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place down under' suggests Australia; it is DIS, the underworld of Roman myth. 'broadcast' is the verb, to scatter.
explanation.definitionFit: To broadcast seed is to scatter it widely, which is to spread it about.

clue.text: A final song from him?

parts.note: last means final
an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: A man's farewell number, the swan song he sings.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is just 'him': a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Alastair is a man's first name, so it can stand for a male person.

clue.text: Circles, missing entrance toestate

indicators.note: missing entrance means the first letter of the estate word is dropped

parts.note: the clue as held runs 'to' and 'estate' together; grounds are the land of an estate

explanation.surface: Rings that have no way into the property.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held fuses 'to estate'; 'missing entrance to' drops the G from GROUNDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Rounds are circular shapes or rings, as in cutting dough into rounds.

clue.text: Came out to corral sheep — it's knotty work!

indicators.note: to corral is to pen livestock, so the scrambled letters enclose the animal
out signals the letters of came are rearranged

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: Someone emerged to round up a sheep, a tricky job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came out' gives MACE, and 'to corral' pens the sheep inside it, splitting it after the third letter. 'knotty' puns on difficult and knotted.
explanation.definitionFit: This craft makes decorative textiles by tying cords in knots, so it is literally knotted work.

clue.text: Those once in fine fettle expire

parts.note: ex means former, once
hale means healthy, in good condition

explanation.surface: People who were formerly healthy breathe their last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expire' looks like 'die', which fits the surface of once-healthy people, but here it means breathe out.
explanation.definitionFit: To expire literally means to breathe out, the opposite of inspire.

clue.text: Spectators follow dog and drive too close

indicators.note: follow puts the spectators' word behind the dog's word

parts.note: to dog someone is to tail them, follow closely
the gate is the number of spectators at a match

explanation.surface: Fans trail behind a dog, and a driver sits on another car's bumper.
explanation.walkthrough: GATE, the attendance at a sports match, is British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: To tailgate is to drive right behind another vehicle, closer than safety allows.

clue.text: Complete book of epistles

definitions.meaning: a church book holding the Epistles and Gospels for the year

explanation.definitionFit: A plenary session is full and attended by all; and a plenary is an old name for a liturgical book of Gospels and Epistles.

clue.text: A social trend may be revealed from these statements

indicators.note: may be revealed suggests the phrase, rearranged, uncovers something new

explanation.surface: Public pronouncements that might expose a pattern in society.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram runs both ways: rearrange 'A social trend' to get the answer, and the answer's letters hide that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A declaration is a formal statement or announcement.

clue.text: Being hospitable, door's open in mess

indicators.note: in puts the scrambled door within the welcoming word

parts.note: warm means friendly and welcoming

indicators.note: open signals that the letters of door are broken up

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: The host is friendly and the door stands open in the dining hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'open' breaks up the door to give DROO, and 'in' lodges that within the friendly word. A wardroom is the officers' mess on a warship.
explanation.definitionFit: On a warship the officers eat and relax in the wardroom, their mess.

clue.text: Church dignitaries leaf over chronicles

indicators.note: over places the page letter above the next piece in this down entry

parts.note: P stands for page, and a page is a leaf of a book
to chronicle is to relate, tell a story

explanation.surface: Someone flips a page over and reads history books.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means the first piece sits on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Prelates are senior clergy such as bishops.

clue.text: May consider a different study of flight

indicators.note: different suggests the letters are made into something else

explanation.surface: Someone might take up a new subject: the science of flying.
explanation.definitionFit: This branch of physics deals with how air flows around moving bodies, the science behind flying.

clue.text: Bird, for example, taking off from branch

parts.note: a diver is a diving water bird, the loon

indicators.note: taking off means rising, so in this down entry the abbreviation reads upwards

parts.note: EG is short for exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A bird, say, takes flight from a tree's limb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'branch' looks like a tree's limb; it is the verb, to fork. 'taking off' turns EG to GE.
explanation.definitionFit: Paths diverge when they split apart in different directions, as they do when they fork.

clue.text: Smart Scots know how to get a bird!

parts.note: chic means stylish, smart
ken is Scots for know

explanation.surface: Clever Scots know how to catch a fowl.
explanation.definitionFit: A domestic fowl, the young hen, is a kind of bird.

clue.text: Front the ballet

definitions.meaning: the face of a building, or a false show
Frederick Ashton's ballet to William Walton's music, first staged in 1931

explanation.definitionFit: A building's face is its façade, and Façade is also the name of Ashton's comic ballet.

clue.text: Conviction? A number set free!

definitions.note: the definition is singular; the answer is the plural, beliefs firmly held

parts.note: ten is a number

indicators.note: free signals the letters of set are let loose and rearranged

explanation.surface: A guilty verdict, yet a group are released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conviction' suggests a court verdict, but it means firm belief. 'free' rearranges SET to ETS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenets are principles firmly held, the beliefs of a creed.

clue.text: Rescue — when digger grabs one — with happy ending!

indicators.note: grabs means the digger's word takes hold of the letter for one

parts.note: a delver is one who digs
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: ending picks out the final letter of happy

explanation.surface: A rescue in which a mechanical digger seizes someone and all ends well.
explanation.definitionFit: Delivery can mean deliverance, being set free or saved from danger.

clue.text: Leaf blight overcoming in the end

indicators.note: overcoming means getting on top of, so the scrambled leaf goes around the little word in
blight means spoil or ruin, so the letters of leaf are broken up

explanation.surface: A disease of foliage finally conquered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaf blight' looks like a plant disease; 'blight' scrambles the leaf to FALE, and 'overcoming' sets it over the little word in.
explanation.definitionFit: A finale is the last part of a show or piece of music, its conclusion.

clue.text: Drop round for the pudding

parts.note: to sag is to droop or drop
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Someone pops over for dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop round' reads as 'call in'; split, it gives SAG and O. Sago pudding is a British milk dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Sago is a starch from palm pith, cooked with milk as a dessert.

clue.text: Hullabaloo following appeal for dismissal

indicators.note: following puts the appeal word behind the dismissal word

parts.note: out is a dismissal in cricket
a cry is an appeal or plea

explanation.surface: An uproar after a cricket fielder's shout for a batter to be given out.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, fielders appeal to the umpire to dismiss a batter, and a dismissed batter is OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcry is a loud public protest, an uproar.

clue.text: After the push given, vehicle reversed — the last in contest

parts.note: to get the push or the sack is to be fired

indicators.note: reversed means the vehicle's word is read backwards

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: last picks the final letter of the word the

explanation.surface: After being fired, someone reverses the car, coming last in a competition.
explanation.walkthrough: SACK and 'the push' are British slang for dismissal from a job. A sack race is a children's race run with both legs inside a sack.
explanation.definitionFit: A sack race is a type of race, run by hopping in a bag, so it is a contest.

clue.text: Round up a lot of peacocks

definitions.meaning: to gather together, assemble troops or people

explanation.definitionFit: To muster troops is to gather them, and a muster is the traditional collective noun for a flock of peacocks.

clue.text: Goes to the bottom, with the beginners

definitions.meaning: those who started or established something

explanation.definitionFit: A ship founders when it fills and sinks; and founders are those who set up an institution.
